utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Witness, I'd just like to clear up one matter. Some witnesses in this case have been referring to the village of Filipovici as Filipovici, and others as Pilipovici, one with an "F," one with a "P." Is there a difference between the two villages or is it the same village?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same village, except that in various documents issued by various institutions, there were differences of that kind, explanations as to whether it's Filipovici or Pilipovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned yesterday that a number of Muslims approached you, seeking protection, and at some stages that it reached to about 500. You mentioned that the first person that arrived seeking protection was a Serb. Do you know the person's name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljuban Blagojevic. His name is Ljuban Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what village was he from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a house in Handzici, where he was supposed to open a restaurant or something like that. However, at any rate, he lived in Handzici, with a predominantly Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you started to house refugees in the compound between the 8th of April and the 26th of April. At any time during that period were you asked to stop protecting the Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked. I was called on the telephone and I was told that I should not receive Muslim civilians any more and that there would be a conflict between the Muslim population in Filipovici and persons who are from Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you receive this phone call? About how many days before the compound was taken over?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometime around the 23rd of April, in the afternoon, a man called Pero called me. He represented the SDS in that area, in the area of Ustikolina, and he told me not to receive refugees any longer, that there would be problems and that there would be clashes between the people from Pilipovici and others, because things that were not normal were happening, things that already belonged to a system of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know Pero's surname?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milisic, something like that. At any rate, one of his legs was shorter. He was a dark man. He was among the head people of the SDS. Mihajlovic. I think it's Pero Mihajlovic, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you told what would happen if you continued to house the Muslims at the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was told -- or actually, Pero told me that he would send people who were paid to cleanse that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you mean "that area," do you mean the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the warehouse and around the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's the JNA warehouse that you were (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he say who he would send to do this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he would send people who were paid to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did he give you any particular reason for making this threat?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave a particular reason, because there was already a conflict above town, near a barracks in a village. That's what he said. And there had already been killings. Some of the Serbs were killed, the Serb population, and at any rate, they wanted to find the culprits and to pay back for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was this man a Serb?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And over this period from the 8th of April to the 26th, what advice were you giving the civilians that were seeking protection at your warehouse?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since these were people who were fleeing from death, they would come to the warehouse, asking to spend the night there, and then logistically speaking, if I can help them in any way - by way of food, that is - then they'd start moving towards Gorazde and a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina where they could avoid the bloodshed. All of those who came could spend unlimited time in the barracks. They could come and leave at the same moment, proceed further on. However, the condition was that they were not allowed to bring weapons into the barracks. If they had any weapons - and they had very few weapons; they mostly had pistols - they would leave it with the soldiers. It would be put in a locker and then, when a man would continue his journey, his weapons would be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And moving to the night of the 25th and the 26th of April, did you hear shooting during that night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is mountainous terrain, in the night between the 25th and 26th, on the 25th already, around 2300 hours, it could be seen at greater distance that there were fires, and already on the 26th, at about 2.00 in the morning, the flames were getting closer to the warehouse and the shooting became louder. From one moment to another, the sound of shooting became louder and louder, which meant that it was getting closer and closer to the warehouse, to the part where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did this shooting continue for, that night and into that morning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shooting continued all night, intermittently. I thought that since this was a religious holiday, a Serb religious holiday, I thought -- I thought that people were celebrating and therefore shooting as well. However, small arms could be heard. However, one could also hear that bigger weapons were being used as well because of these flashes of light, because such flashes certainly cannot come from small-calibre weapons. They have to come from larger-calibre weapons. So one can assume that these were attacks with larger-calibre weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about what time did this shooting and these larger-calibre weapons stop firing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The firing from these larger-calibre weapons abated sometime in the morning of the 26th, and then nearby, there was shooting and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did some of the refugees or the civilians seeking protection at the warehouse, did they leave that morning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Refugees started leaving already in -- on the 25th, during the night, and that number kept going down every minute. I did not monitor the exact number of people as it went down from one hour to the other; however, the front line was getting closer, moving towards the warehouse. People were going towards Gorazde, towards the rest of the free territory. So already in the morning, this number was very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people were in the compound at the warehouse when it was taken over later that day? About how many refugees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were about 50 refugees left, a bit more than that, primarily women, children, and those who could not go on because they were disabled or ill. In addition to that, they thought that whatever would happen to the regular army, the Yugoslav People's Army, could happen to them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, this group of people that was still there before the compound was taken over, did you move them within the compound to a safer place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were snipers already at the small building by the entrance into the warehouse. First, I had to withdraw the soldier who was there at the entrance, guarding the entrance. There was already shelling, shooting around the warehouse. When I saw that, then in order to save the refugees, I moved them about 70 metres from headquarters to a storage area, which is an underground storage area, and that was safe if the warehouse itself were to be shelled, so that these people would not get killed. I also put two soldiers there to guard them; if possible, to defend them with rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And later that day, did soldiers, other soldiers, others than your own, break into the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 1300 hours, the White Eagles, with their formations, broke through the gate of the warehouse and barged into the warehouse itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at this time, were you in the administration building, in the command centre?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only two soldiers and I remained at the command centre. All the other soldiers and refugees were in the shelter that I mentioned a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the White Eagles, where are they from? Where is that unit based?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, these are mercenaries who came from Serbia. That's a paramilitary formation that did not belong to any one of the armies. The JNA had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many broke into the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 20 of them. They came in a bulletproof vehicle. It was about as big as a small freight vehicle. And in the front and in the back it had thick metal sheets that could protect from any profile of bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after they broke into the compound, did you speak to the commander of this group at any time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the commander, when they broke in with this bulletproof vehicle, they came to the very entrance of the command. They asked me to talk. They said that they were regular army. So there was a meeting between myself and them. They said to two of my soldiers that we had to negotiate, otherwise they would kill all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many people did you speak to from the White Eagles at this time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were they the -- was one of them, at least, the commander of that group?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to Commander Dida and his brother Vlado. Those were the only names I knew. I didn't find out about any other names until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And on this day, was this the first time that you met Dida and Vlado?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you know those were their names?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that those were their names because Vlado said, "Dida, call the boss to see what we'll do with the main guy at headquarters and what we'll do with the rest." And Dida then called; using a Motorola, he called the boss, who ordered them to bring me in. As for the rest, they could do whatever they deemed necessary. This conversation took place in the office where I was the only person, together with Dida and Vlado. Dida often addressed Vlado, and Vlado often addressed Dida, and they used their names most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was discussed between Dida and Vlado and yourself?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when Dida entered my office, which was supposed to be the office of the commander of barracks, he took a Motorola and he called the boss. He said, when speaking on the Motorola, he said, "Number 90 speaking," and then his boss came in. I don't know what number he used. And he asked him, "What should we do with this main guy here?" That was me. And then he asked what he should do with the rest. He said -- I heard this boss of theirs speaking on the Motorola, saying, "Bring that main guy in here and do whatever you want with the rest." After that, Dida asked me where the refugees were, and I answered that I did not have any refugees. In the meantime, a team of the White Eagles - actually, those who had come with Vlado and Dida - got out of the armoured vehicle, and they were already all over headquarters and in the warehouse. Dida said to me that if I do not say where the refugees are, they would set the warehouse on fire and that we'd burn in it, both we and the refugees. Since I had no choice, in order to save human lives, at least to a certain extent, that is to say of soldiers and of refugees, I said where the refugees were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you stated where the refugees were, did you hear anything? Did you hear any gunfire?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First Dida's and Vlado's soldiers in the headquarters forced all the strongboxes open and took whatever they wanted, and then when they learnt where the refugees were, Dida and two of his men went to the refugees. I stayed in the office where I was guarded by Vlado, who was with me. And after a while, I heard two relatively long bursts of fire, because my field of vision from the headquarters was such that I could not see what was going on in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you hear later whether any refugees died that day in the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, because I did not leave the office or know what was going on until around 1700, when we were to go to Foca. Only after I came out, I saw that soldiers were in the armoured vehicle and that a bus had come to take women and children on. In that column, there were many cars that had been in the depot and which the White Eagles took away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At about 5.00, were the refugees placed on the bus?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 5.00, I saw a bus that was full but I did not know how many refugees were in it and how many refugees were taken, nor did I dare ask about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you taken from the compound to the Velecevo women's prison shortly afterwards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, at the head of the column were representatives of the White Eagles. Then behind them, a column was formed and I was in it, and refugees and troops and the cars, all the cars that had been found in the depot - they were private cars - and we set off towards Foca. But we were stopped at the intersection 15 metres from the barracks as a car had been set on fire there, a small Fiat, and we all had to get off the vehicle because gunfire took place. And after that, one of men -- one of White Eagles came up to me, pulled out his knife and he said, "That's the balija. I'll cut his throat now." And at that moment, a White Eagle - Vlado, Dida, I don't know which - said, "You won't." And I only got a rifle butt on my head. Fifteen minutes later, since the snipers had stopped their fire, the column proceeded towards Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were your soldiers also taken from the compound as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All soldiers were taken from the depot in a vehicle which had brought the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the vehicle that you were in, who else was with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a jeep which belonged to me, and I had a driver with me and two men, two White Eagles whom I do not know. It was the first time I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after this incident when you were hit, were you taken to Velecevo women's prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were the refugees taken there as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. In Foca, the vehicles parted ways. I was taken to Velecevo and other vehicles stayed in Foca, and where they went from there, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the women's prison, about?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you arrived at the prison, were you handed over to anyone?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They handed us - me - over to the prison guard, and the guards took me to the second floor, to a room at the very entrance into the Velecevo penitentiary; rather, the area of Velecevo. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And before you went inside the prison, did you see any other soldiers or other guards on your arrival?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard was -- the guards were at the entrance, at the gate. The guards were around the gate. And in front of it, on an elevation in front of the gate, Serb troops were lined up, those who were coming back from a mission. To my mind -- or rather, I guessed that there were around 30, more than 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what were they wearing, these troops?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you know they were Serb troops?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, well, had they been regular soldiers, they would have had olive-grey uniforms; and again, the caps were different. Neither the clothes nor the patches on their shoulders, they were already theirs; that is, they were different from those of the Yugoslav People's Army. Be that as it may, those were troops which did not belong to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were taken -- you were handed over to guards and taken inside the prison, taken to a room. I'd now like to ask you, when you first arrived in that room, who you saw there. Not what happened, but who you saw in that room.

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty guard or the duty soldier - depends on what you call them - took me to the first floor, to the third room on the right -- on the left, and I entered. And in that room I saw Vojo Maksimovic; Velibor Ostojic; Cancar; then a man with a pimple, pimples, rather short, and later on I realised he was a physician; and a man with white hair, medium height, and rather skinny.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did anyone else come into this room shortly after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And their chief also entered the room, Simkovic. No. No. No. Stanic. Stanic came. Miro Stanic came two or three minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you first arrived in this room, was there a table in it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two tables. Both were close by. One could consider them as one table; bigger, much bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you see on those tables?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were large topographic maps on the table, quite large.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to see what the maps were of, what areas they were of?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the -- one of them showed the area towards Ustikolina, towards Gorazde, and the other showed Foca and the upper part, towards Velecevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see any markings on those maps?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On these maps there were marked units. There were red and blue colours. And some facilities, that is, areas, were circled. Whatever the case, it could -- one could realise straight away that those were units which were attacking, that is, units which were defending themselves, or rather, the capture of some facilities and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what colour these markings were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red and blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see the village of Filipovici on one of these maps?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the village of Pilipovici circled, and a date. That is that day, the 26th, the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in this room, did you see anything on the walls?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the wall, there was another map showing the territory of Foca, a large one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you came into the room, what happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Vojo Maksimovic knew me, that is he knew the family, he said, "Where do you come from, 120? How did you turn up here? I had just arrived from Belgrade, and I don't know anything about what is going on here." And I told him that those maps offered sufficient information as to what was going on, and on the -- and the fact that I had been brought up there. Ostojic asked me, "Have you joined balijas and Ustasha too? And we'll find out how much you've helped them." And Cancar just waved his hand like that, as a sign that something would happen in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you respond to Ostojic when he said, "Have you joined the balijas and Ustashas too?"

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not reply anything specifically but I did say, "We'll see what will happen next."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that a Miro Stanic came into the room shortly after you arrived. Did he say anything when he came in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miro asked, "And what is this one doing here?" To which he added, -- to which Vojo Maksimovic added, "Never mind, slowly." And meanwhile, because this office was connected with the Miro Stanic's office, an active-duty military came through the door through which I had come, Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Ivanic [as interpreted], as far as I can remember. It was an active-duty military in the Yugoslav People's Army. And he said, "Is that the commander?" And turned towards them and said, "If I'm wrong, let them court-martial me in Sarajevo or in Belgrade," to let the refugees go, because they bore no responsibility for anything, and if they killed me, as he was a Serb, a true Serb, born in Serbia, and had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina by May 15th, that he would write about my murder and the killing of refugees at some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You stated that this Ivancic said if they kill you, and if they kill the refugees, he would write about this. That hadn't -- in your evidence so far, that hasn't been mentioned, that any of the people in the room had said that you would be killed or the refugees would be killed. Do you know why Ivancic said that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he knew that something would happen to us, and as an active-duty military in the Yugoslav People's Army, under the Geneva Conventions, the oath of allegiance he had taken, he could not harm any people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After Ivancic said this, warned others to not kill you or the refugees, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After -- what happened after that was that I left, that Miro Stanic said that I would be transferred to Sarajevo the next day for court-martial, and that he would see about the refugees. After that, they sent me to the lower floor by the entrance to have the wound I had on my head examined, and because it wasn't bleeding much, the skin had only burst, I was brought back some 20 minutes later to the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were brought back, do you remember who was in the room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that room were Vojo Maksimovic, Ostojic and Cancar, and that one who had told me to go and see about the wound, that medical man - I suppose it was that physician - and another man, white-haired, thin. And Miro Stanic was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were brought back to the room, was there a further conversation with any of these men?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojo Maksimovic told me, "Welcome, 120, 120. You must have a drink with us." I said I couldn't, but they said that it was a Serb custom and therefore one had to. So they poured some brandy for me, and after a while, I said, "Cheers," and drank a small glass of brandy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know why you were offered a drink?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first I thought -- I thought that the worst would happen, as always when the worst judgement is passed, and I thought that something very bad would happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during this time that you were in the room for the second time, was there any conversation with any of the men in the room, apart from offering you this drink, about what would happen to you or the refugees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that I would be brought to justice in Sarajevo, to which I answered that I refused -- that I wouldn't go to Sarajevo because I would have to pass through the area of Miljevina, where a very mean paramilitary formation was which operated under its own discretion, had no command over it, and because of that, I was sure I would never reach Sarajevo alive. So I said, "You better kill me straight away." And I forgot to say that this Lieutenant Colonel Jovic [as interpreted] was also present there. And to which he said, "Well, then they will take me to court in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that they said you would be taken to Sarajevo to be brought to justice. Do you remember who particularly said that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Velibor Ostojic say anything whilst you were in that room on the second time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from what he said in the beginning, Velibor did not anything new of any interest [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in this room on the second time, and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all in all, about two hours, with going downstairs about the wound and so on and so forth; and after that, I was taken to the room opposite where there was no one, to await my further fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so when you left this room for the second time, how was the discussion left? You mentioned that you were told that you would be taken to Sarajevo to be brought to justice. Was that how the conversation was left or was any further details given to you about what would happen to you and the refugees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not supply me with any detail. They said, "You're coming here," and the guard escorted me to another room. And I did not know what was in store for me, and even less so what was in store for the refugees, apart from the promise given by Lieutenant Colonel Ivancic that the refugees had to be set free, that they had to be set free and that I had to be taken to court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you were placed in this other room for a few hours, were you taken to the KP Dom in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'd just like now to ask you a few brief questions about the people that you met in the room. Did you know Vojislav Maksimovic before this night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did he do, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a teacher in Sarajevo. He taught in Sarajevo, and in Sarajevo he advocated peaceful, that is, good cohabitation of Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and all the other ethnic groups. He was brought up -- he grew up in a family which was tolerant when it came to good relations among different ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was he a politician?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For which party?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned you saw Velibor Ostojic in the room. Did you know him before this night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Velibor Ostojic from the media, because he was the minister of information in radio/television of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I knew him by sight. After he left his flat in Ilidza because of a fight, he came to live near me, so that we met unofficially a number of times. He was on the same level as the people who were at the top of the political ladder in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know whether he belonged to any political party?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, according to the media, that he belonged to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you saw a Miro Stanic in the room that night. Did you know him before you arrived at Velecevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Milorad Stanic in my life, although he was in Foca. I never had any contacts with him before that night, nor did I ever see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that -- earlier you mentioned his name was Miro Stanic and a moment ago you mentioned Milorad. What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first I found out that his name was Miro Stanic. However, later, I found out that this was Milorad Stanic. However, at that moment, in the period up to 1995, I only knew that he was Miro Stanic. At any rate, he was the man in charge up there at Velecevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At any rate, how did you know that his name was Stanic? Did you hear that that night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it that night when Lieutenant Colonel Ivanic [as interpreted] Personally addressed Stanic and said, "Commander Stanic, you have to take this man to court, and you have to release all the refugees." When somebody is addressed as "Commander," then that person is the person in charge, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you find out his first name was Miro that night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out because Vojo Maksimovic and Cancar called him that. Cancar once also said Miro. So I remember that name. I don't know whether it's a pet name or something like that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned a Milan Ivancic, a Lieutenant Colonel Milan Ivancic, that you met that night in that room. Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a military uniform, olive-green/grey, of the Yugoslav People's Army. He had rank insignia showing that he was a Lieutenant Colonel. And this is what it looks like. There are gold lines around the epaulette and two golden stars. That denotes the rank of Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you know that his name was Milan Ivancic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, he introduced himself. When he was in the room, he said, "My name is so and so." I don't know whether that is his name or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you find out that night where he was based?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Velecevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that you saw a Petko Cancar in the room. Did you know him from before that night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him by sight. I saw him once in Sarajevo. I did not know him personally. I had no contacts with him because the nature of my work did not require that. I know that he was some kind of a politician in the municipal structures. I also know that he was in the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there was a physician in the room. Did you know his name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no. I don't know. He was a medium-height man, a man of medium height, plumpish, with pimples. I don't know his name but they did address him as "Doctor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There was a doctor before who had pimples who was skinny. This is a different one, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We are not completely sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Having interrupted you, why are we spending so much time on this particular incident? Is it for some other case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's for this case, Your Honour, in terms of showing the combination of the military and the civil government and how they worked together, and more so for the widespread and systematic aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Upon the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, this man wasn't a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This witness? No, no, but just in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can understand the relevance of it but I'm wondering why it is necessary to spend so much time on it. Why don't we get into the KP Dom, with which we really are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that's where we are about to head right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank heavens for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what time did you leave the Velecevo prison that night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime before 2.00 at night, and I arrived at the KP Dom a bit after 3.00, about ten past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who took you there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken there by two men I did not know, and a driver, a driver who drove me, who drove me to Velecevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The two men, were they from Velecevo, that took you there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Velecevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that two White Eagles took you to Velecevo. Did they also escort you to the KP Dom, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these are different ones, different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the KP Dom, what did you see on the outside of the building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the building, at the very entrance, there was a bus full of women and children. I was on one side, and on the other side, next to me, was this driver. There were two men who I did not know. There was Dida and Vlado. There were three other men. Later on, I found out that they were from the KP Dom. Among them was Krnojelac as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This person that you mentioned as Krnojelac, when did you learn -- did you know him from before, before you saw him out the front of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you learn this person's name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned it when I entered the KP Dom, the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did this man tell you his name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when he told you his name, how did you believe it was spelled, from how he stated it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is Krnojevac. That was my understanding then, and that's how I remembered that last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did this Krnojevac, did he tell you his first name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krnojevac, Mico. However, Krnojelac Milorad is his real name, was his real name. At that time, I thought it was Mico Krnojevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, could you spell the name that this person told you, what his surname was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: K-r-n-o-j-e-v-a-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the entrance at the front of the KP Dom, and you saw this bus, I think with women and children in it, were they the refugees from Filipovici?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were they on the bus or were they outside of it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And your soldiers, did you know where they were at that stage?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where was this Krnojevac and this Dida and Vlado? Where were they in relation to the entrance to the KP Dom when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were three to four metres away from the entrance into the room of the KP Dom. There was a heated debate and there was shooting into the air. Dida then asked those three, or rather said that if he was not paid on that day, that he would kill the entire bus, that he would take it down below the hospital and kill all the refugees. One of these three from the KP Dom said Dida had been intoxicated, and Vlado was standing next to him and trying to pacify him. One of those three, probably Krnojevac, said, "Ask the boss about taking the bus. Use your Motorola." Dida's brother, Vlado, grabbed Dida by the hand in which he held his Motorola, telling him not to call because he would get into trouble with the boss. After that, when he saw that he should not call, they set out towards the entrance of the KP Dom and the bus with the refugees remained outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dida. Dida. Dida was doing the shooting. He was shooting into the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how long did this discussion go on for?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly. Five minutes perhaps, at maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened at the end of this discussion? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of this discussion it was said, it was proposed -- I mean, these people from the KP Dom said, "Let's go inside and we'll discuss this." They withdrew into a room that in my view was the office of the warden of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was this room on the ground floor or on a floor above it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ground floor. Ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as you went into the entrance to the KP Dom, did you turn right or left to get to this room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Right. We turned to the right, and this room was on the left, the first room on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you remember who said, "Let's go inside"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of those three from the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned that Krnojevac, you believed, was from the KP Dom. The other two, did you know their names?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know their names, but they were present throughout this conversation. They were there, the KP Dom, in the office, together with Krnojevac, during those moments while I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This Krnojevac, did he acknowledge you whilst the discussion was being had between himself, the other two, and Dida and Vlado, outside of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course he was aware of the entire situation. As soon as it was decided not to take the bus, or rather when Dida said that he will tell the driver to take the bus below the hospital and that he would kill all of them, and then he was told he should call the boss, there was the possibility of negotiating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these two men that took you from Velecevo to the KP Dom, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you went inside, into this office, who was in there? I think you mentioned Krnojevac, the other two men. And who else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dida and Vlado and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened when you were inside this office?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A heated debate started concerning the refugees and what should be done and whether that would be paid or not. Dida was very angry. Vlado tried to pacify him. As far as I can remember, he even fired a burst of gunfire through the window in his anger. He said, "What do we need this balija here for?" In order for me not to get killed, or even something worse than that, then Krnojevac said that I should be put into the third room, away from his office, until this situation calmed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was that third room on the same floor as the office you went into?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Also on the left-hand side. This was a room where there were big tables for dining. I was on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said the heated debate continued in this office when you first arrived. Who was the debate between?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krnojevac, Dida, Vlado, and two of these men who were from the KP Dom. Those were the people concerned. Nobody else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were in that office on the first occasion, was the phone ringing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was anyone answering the phone?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For the most part, telephone lines were interrupted then, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how long did this heated debate take before you were taken out of the room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about seven or eight minutes while I was present, and after that, I was taken out. Afterwards, only clamouring could be heard, but I can't give you anything in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that Krnojevac suggested that you should be put into the third room. Did someone take you there or did Krnojevac take you there? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. One of his men, one of the men who was in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these other two men, what were they wearing? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian clothes. They had civilian clothes, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was Krnojevac wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he wore a military uniform, olive-green/grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that these three men, including Krnojevac, seemed to come from the KP Dom. Were you able to say who was more superior out of the three, if at all?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could. I think that Krnojevac was at the highest level compared to those two, because I saw that they obeyed his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what orders are you referring to? You mentioned that he said that you should be taken to another room and you were taken by one of those men. Are there any other orders that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw that when they tried to pacify Dida, that they were helping their boss in this pacification, et cetera. I also think that since they were sitting on the side, that they, at any rate, are lower down the ladder than Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were taken into this second room, about how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometime around 6.00, so it was about 40 minutes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at some time were you called back to the office that Krnojevac was in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was called back and then I was offered coffee. And then Krnojevac said that he knew both brothers, that he was a mathematics teacher, that he knew them but not me, because I came to Foca very seldom. He also said that he had two sons and that he was working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he say what those two sons did?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When did Krnojevac introduce himself that evening or that morning to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was over coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you had coffee with Krnojevac, was anyone else in the room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two men of his who were sitting there. From time to time, somebody would walk in and go out, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Dida and Vlado, where were they at this time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. After this pacification, after this situation that took place in the office, I did not see them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did Krnojevac mention anything about the refugees whilst you were having coffee?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krnojevac said that the refugees had entered the KP Dom, that they were in the KP Dom, and he said that since there were a lot of small children, that "I tried to go to Velecevo to get them milk." Those are his words. I heard -- while I was in the room that night, I could hear footsteps, but I did not think that they were getting in and that they would be accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I believe it's time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you mentioned that about 6.00 in the morning, you were invited back to the office of Krnojevac and you had a coffee with this person, and the other, the two men you felt were his subordinates were in that room. And you mentioned that he stated to you who he was and that he was a math teacher and he had two sons, that he knew your brothers, and that he tried to get some milk for the children, the women and children. And you also said that he entered -- that the women -- he said that the women and children had entered the KP Dom. Did he say what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said -- he then said that soldiers and I would be put up in a part of the KP Dom in the restaurant, or rather above the restaurant in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was that restaurant inside the KP Dom or outside of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the KP Dom, but with guards. I mean, there were guards around the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did he tell you how long you were going to stay there, why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said -- he did not say how long we were going to stay, and what -- and that it would be decided what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just from your observations of Krnojevac that morning, what did you think his role was at the KP Dom, just from your observations?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my observations, it was a person who must have been one of the front men in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "front men," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean one of chief persons, main chiefs in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To that conclusion led me the fact that since he put -- put the refugees in the KP Dom, and if he could guarantee that he would do certain things, and since he frequently went to Velecevo because of the farm - that is what he said - I thought that was the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What did he say he did at Velecevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he was going to the farm, to supply that area with food, and that he had some appointments up there at Velecevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were invited back into the room for coffee with Krnojevac and these two other men, what do you think the purpose of that discussion was, from what was said between both of you? What do you think Krnojevac's purpose was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Krnojevac's purpose was to inform me, because this Lieutenant Colonel had said that the soldiers had to be set free and sent home. And his purpose was to try to learn what would happen next, what would happen to the refugees, according to the orders of this Lieutenant Colonel, what would happen next to the soldiers, what would happen next to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who informed you that the Lieutenant Colonel had said that -- I think you said the Lieutenant Colonel said that the soldiers had to be set free; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you -- which Lieutenant Colonel are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That one, Ivanic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he tell you that or did Krnojevac tell you that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that. I did not mention it in my statement, but he told me when we were up there at Velecevo. He said that the soldiers would be set free, that they were soldiers who had completed their military service and that they should go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the particular mood of this discussion between yourself and Krnojevac that morning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mood was that of giving orders. Since he said, "Commander Miro Stanic, I'm going back to Velecevo. You should take this man to court in Sarajevo. You are to set refugees free and send the soldiers back home."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I meant the mood of the discussion between yourself and Krnojevac that morning, when he was giving information about himself and what would happen to the refugees and the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular, regular conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did the discussion end, the one in which you had the coffee?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conversation ended by my going back to that room again, and after that, around 7.00, they came to fetch me again because my brother from Sarajevo had called by telephone, and Krnojevac said, "Here is your brother. Talk to your brother. Here's your brother. And tell him, let him tell you that he is safe and sound," because in Sarajevo, there has Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already been information that the barracks had been set on fire, that the Green Berets had taken the barracks and that I had been taken in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the barracks you're referring to is the warehouse at Filipovici, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The depot, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who came to this other room that you were in to take you into the office where Krnojevac was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man, the man who was sitting with Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you say to your brother?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was safe and sound, and he said, "What are you doing in the KP Dom?" "I don't know." "We have been notified in Sarajevo," he said, "that the Green Berets had taken the warehouse, in the media, and that most men had been killed." And that was the end of the conversation between my brother and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after the phone call, was there any discussion between yourself and Krnojevac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, except that the soldiers and I would be put up in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that P61A be placed in front of the witness. We have a copy here. It's the plan of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at this plan, this is the plan of the KP Dom, the building at the front and the detention facilities for the prisoners at the back. Is that plan familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you point out with the pointer the entrance that you went into that night, of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, he indicates the left-hand entrance to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you point out with the pointer the room, the office that you went into on the first occasion with Dida, Vlado, Krnojevac, and the other two men?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, he indicates the first office to the right of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you indicate the other room that you were taken to for that longer period of time before you were asked back for a coffee?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness indicates the third office from the right, and it's Soba number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. We're finished with that map now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that Krnojevac told you that yourself and the soldiers would be put up into the restaurant. You said the restaurant was outside the KP Dom. I will show you a photograph, and can you tell me whether or not you see the restaurant which you were placed inside - the top one, thanks - that morning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Exhibit P18 and it's the top photograph. I think it's 00407443 - sorry - 42. And the witness indicates with the pointer the white building on the right-hand side with -- it's difficult to see on that one, but the word "restaurant" on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Immediately to the right of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. We're finished with that photograph now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Krnojevac leave with you as you left the administration building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who else left with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His men, one of his men - dark, youngish - one who was in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you taken to the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started to the restaurant with him, and Krnojevac went in a car towards Foca and he said, "I'm off to the farm."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I asked you this question earlier, but what was Krnojevac wearing during this night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Olive-green/grey uniform, working uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is this a military uniform or a civilian uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military. That's the military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is this the uniform of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there any insignia on this uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know whether Krnojevac had a firearm on his uniform that night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what type of firearm was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a belt and a pistol on the right-hand side, in a holster.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you were taken to this restaurant. Were your soldiers that were at Filipovici, were they at the restaurant at that stage?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this restaurant wasn't being used as a restaurant at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lower part was once used as a restaurant, but I did not see what the lower part was being used for. And the upper floor were bedrooms where people could sleep in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that's where you were kept; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the soldiers as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After you saw Krnojevac that morning, about 7.00 that morning, did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see him on that day or sometime later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were taken to the KP Dom on the early morning of the 27th. Do you mean, then, that you saw Krnojevac on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th. Yes, the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you get to see him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he came to the room where I was and said that the refugees would be allowed to go during the day, that he knew nothing about me and the soldiers, and that the Lieutenant Colonel would try to settle the matter, and that he had provided the milk for refugees' children. As these soldiers were there, I asked when will they go home, but he could not give me any answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when he said that the Lieutenant Colonel will sort out the matter in relation to the soldiers, did he say which Lieutenant Colonel?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That one that was at Velecevo, Ivanic [as interpreted]; Milan Ivanic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was he wearing when you spoke to him on this day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did this discussion last?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from the way he spoke, could you work out the reason why he approached you and advised you of what was happening to the refugees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the order of Lieutenant Colonel Ivanic [as interpreted] and the Yugoslav People's Army was still in force, and I thought that some orders had to be complied with. Besides, I thought that what Lieutenant Colonel Ivanic [as interpreted] had said in front of Miro Stanic, that some day, sooner or later, it would be revealed what had happened to the refugees and me. I think that was the reason why he did what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, you mentioned that the time that you saw Krnojevac in relation to this incident was on the 27th of April, the same day that you were taken to the restaurant. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain it. On the 27th, at 3.00 in the morning, I was brought to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The question I'm asking you is: Can you explain why it appears in the statement that you saw Krnojevac at the restaurant on the 27th and today you've mentioned that you saw him on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement is not correct. The date is not correct. I didn't look at the statement, because the refugees were set free the next day, and it was the next day that I saw Krnojevac, on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After seeing Krnojevac at the restaurant on this day, have you ever seen him again?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how old was this Milorad Krnojevac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forty-ish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what colour was his hair?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what shall I say? Light, light -- light brown, and some white hair. That is, brown hair with white hairs, mixed with white hairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was it long or short, the hair?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Short, short.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was it a full head of hair? Was it slightly receding or how was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his hair was receding slightly and, to be quite honest, he didn't have much hair. His hair was receding quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know how tall he was in relation to your height?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about -- I'm 180 and he is also somewhere around that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what type of build did he have? Fat, thin?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medium, medium. Neither fat nor thin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you remember anything particular other than that about his appearance?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had round cheeks, regular nose, and I don't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise this person if you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I could do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In your first statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, your meetings with this Milorad Krnojevac weren't mentioned, but they were mentioned in your second statement. Why is that? Why were they not mentioned in the first statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of statements by men who interrogated me about what I had said, that is talked. They took out some fragments and insisted on fragments, insisting that that had been the way that I had put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not clear, but in your first statement, the meetings with Krnojevac were not mentioned. Why is that? The first statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did give it, but -- as far as I can remember, I did mention this detail, and they said, "Well, sign this, because this is what interests us." And I told the whole story as I am telling it now in court, except that some details came back to me, or they told me to reflect more about some other details, to see if they were right or not, because after a long time has passed and one forgets. And besides, whenever you are in a situation, when you're afraid ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever you are in a situation when you are afraid, one simply doesn't see a whole ocean of things. All he thinks about is how to keep his life. He doesn't really pay much attention to what somebody looks like and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did you stay in this restaurant building? For about how many days?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were at that restaurant building, were you taken for interrogations at Velecevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how often were you taken over that period?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what questions were being asked of you, very briefly, in those interrogations?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you very briefly: Who I cooperated with, how much I helped Muslims in terms of ammunition, weapons, food, clothes, footwear and sanitary supplies, and also who these people who were around the warehouse were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you ever beaten during those interrogations at Velecevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was beaten once at the captain's. He was basically a bald man. I don't know who this man was, his bodyguard or something. After we talked, after there were lots of questions, when I was asked how many weapons I had given and food and things like that, then he said, "You're going to tell us everything." And he hit me so bad that I simply flew into the corner. In the meantime, a few minutes later, five or six minutes later, Lieutenant Colonel Ivanic [as interpreted] came, and when he saw what had happened, he said he wasn't supposed to do that kind of thing to me. Most times when I went out of the KP Dom, they drove me in a jeep. Sometimes they just gave me a ride through Foca so that the people who had remained would realise, I guess --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I don't know -- I don't know whether the Prosecutor has the right to interrupt the witness. The witness started to talk and he had not even finished his sentence and he was given the sign to stop. He didn't finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He had in fact, I think, given four or five sentences. I think that an examiner is entitled, if he feels that the witness is straying, to bring him back to the subject, if that's what you were doing, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That was the only purpose, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The actual terms of your interruption don't appear in the transcript, but that is what I thought you were doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. I did not think that the Prosecutor had had any ill intentions or something like that. I just wondered how the witness would finish his sentence. The Defence is not suspicious in any way. We are aware of the good intentions involved, but we just wondered how the witness would finish his sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you think that it's relevant in some way, you can ask him in cross-examination. And you have the ability there to ask leading questions. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was conducting the interrogations at Velecevo? From what military unit were these people from or this person from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person was -- was in Velecevo. He had a uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army. He was a balding man. He cooperated together with the others. I don't know what post he held or what his position was within the formation concerned, within the establishment. I only know that he was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were at the restaurant, who guarded it, for this nine-day period?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That restaurant, I mean there was a duty man there. There were two policemen in front in a kiosk. On three sides, there were machine-gun nests. On the left-hand side, there was one facing the bridge, and the other one was by the upper gate, and the third one was to the left of the restaurant. Those machine-gun nests actually had sacks surrounding them, and they were manned by four to six men, depending on the situation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these policemen that were in front, in a kiosk, were they policemen from the town of Foca or were they attached to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were men from the KP Dom, and often they were joined by some of the policemen from town. My room was in such a position that I could not see very well whether these were policemen from the KP Dom or from town. I can't really tell you that. For the most part, it was two or three men, so it would be someone from the KP Dom and then they would be joined by someone from town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, you stated that you left the restaurant, and were you taken to the command centre of the JNA in Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long were you kept there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you speak to Lieutenant Colonel Milan Ivancic whilst you were at Ustikolina, at the command centre?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came around the 10th, 10th of May, to tell me that I would be taken to court in Belgrade. While as far as the soldiers are concerned, a bus came on the 7th of May and transferred them to Titograd, all those soldiers except for two soldiers who were from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did Lieutenant Colonel Ivancic tell you about what was happening to the JNA, the JNA units at Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did the JNA units at Ustikolina leave at this period?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most did and -- most had left and it was Serb soldiers who came in. It was already on the 7th that the barracks were handed over. That's when the barracks were handed over, so that the reservists and the Serb soldiers would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So the barracks were handed over to Serb forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were at Ustikolina, you were beaten on one occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 13th of May, because on the 13th of May the ammunitions and explosives storage was transferred. Ammunition and explosive devices were taken away every day in vehicles with Niksic licence plates, and on the 13th of May the entire warehouse had definitely been removed, all the ammunition and the mines and explosive devices. They had a banquet in a restaurant near the warehouse, and then they said that I could go there together with them to this banquet. Thanks to a soldier, an ethnic Serb who had already been at the front line in the area of Dubrovnik - his first name was Obrad - he said to me, "It's better for you to get killed than to go up there and get massacred." I didn't go there. I was beaten, I was trampled upon, I was dragged around, so that I could go up there after all, but when they realised that he was a full-blooded person and that things could not be done that way, they returned me to the office of commander Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was it a soldier that beat you or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two soldiers from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And on the 15th of May you went to the Velecevo prison, and then from there you went to Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with an escort in Velecevo, thanks to the Lieutenant Colonel, who said I had to go on the 15th to Belgrade; I'm not a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina; if I don't go on the 15th, I'll be a war criminal. He said that I should be given an escort and a certificate, which I got, that I was going to court to Belgrade. So I was escorted via Scepan Polje to Titograd, and then yet another escort took me from Titograd to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you stayed in Belgrade for a number of days and then you left to a third country; is that correct? Just yes or no will do.

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you a few questions about the theoretical and practical military training that a JNA reserve officer of the rank Captain First Class would require to hold that rank in the former JNA system. First, I assume that a person of this rank would be required to do their compulsory military service; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how long is the compulsory military service in the JNA system?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120 [Resumed]
